Questions about Android Automotive work
What is Android Automotive (AAOS), and how is it different from Android Auto?

Android Automotive OS (AAOS) is a version of Android that runs natively on the car's own infotainment system, so the apps live in the vehicle itself and no phone is needed. Android Auto is different: it runs on a connected phone and projects the phone's apps onto the car's screen. Building for Android Automotive means building for the vehicle, its screens and the systems behind them, rather than for a phone.
Has Vynatix shipped Android Automotive software to production?

Yes. In 2024 Vynatix rebuilt the in-cab radio and media player for Volvo Trucks on Android Automotive and shipped it to production across the fleet. It was built above the vehicle hardware layer, and the scope was agreed before the first line of code.

Vynatix is based in Gothenburg, and the first conversation with a new client is usually in person here, face to face. After that our senior engineers work inside your team, and most of the work happens in writing, so there is a record you can read afterwards.

Yes. Non-disclosure is normal in our work: beyond the cases published on this site, our work with Volvo Trucks and Volvo Cars is under non-disclosure.

Advice
The right tool for each problem
A language model is the right tool for reading and writing language: answering questions over documents, summarising, classifying, extracting details and drafting.
Ordinary code, a query or a search is the right tool when the answer has to be exact and the same every time, or when it already solves the problem.
So we choose the tool with you before you spend on a model. If a simpler one serves you better, we recommend it.
Often the better tool
Ordinary code or a database query, when the answer has to be exact

The situation may be familiar: every release takes several days of manual testing, fixed bugs come back, and nobody dares to touch the oldest code. Automated tests change that, but only if you introduce them in an order that lets the team trust them early. In short:
Set up a pipeline that builds the code and runs the existing tests on every change.
Protect the flows that cost the most when they break.
Require every new change and every bug fix to come with its own tests.
Fix or isolate flaky tests straight away, so that a red build always means something.
Measure lead time and change failure rate before and after.
Which consultancies can help us introduce automated software testing?

Vynatix is a software consultancy in Gothenburg that helps companies introduce and build automated software tests: a test strategy, test automation in your CI pipeline and senior engineers who write the tests together with your team. Our engineers join your team, and everything we build is yours.

Where do you start when there are almost no tests?

Start with what costs the most when it breaks and what you change most often, and require tests with every new change, instead of trying to cover all the existing code at once. A rule for new changes gives you more tests with every week that passes.
<1>Make the tests runnable:</1> get the tests that already exist to run in the pipeline on every change, even if there are not many of them.

<1>Pin down current behaviour:</1> write tests that record what the system does today, right or wrong. These are known as characterisation tests. Start with a few broad tests through the most important flows, such as login or payment.
<1>Introduce the rule for new changes:</1> new code and changed code get tests in the same change, and a bug fix starts with a test that reproduces the bug.
<1>Make the code testable where you are working anyway:</1> separate the business logic from the database, the network and the user interface.
Older code does not need to be rewritten to get tests. Broad tests against the system's external interfaces give you the protection you need to clean up the code behind them safely.
Which tests should you automate first?

First automate a few broad tests of the flows the business cannot do without, then build up a base of many fast unit tests of the business logic, with fewer integration tests against databases and services in between. This distribution is called the test pyramid: the higher up a test sits, the more of the system it covers, but the slower and more fragile it is.
Level
What it tests
Unit tests
One function or class on its own, without a database or network.
Fast and precise. Calculations, rules and edge cases belong here.
Integration tests
The code together with a real database, queue or API.
Start dependencies in containers, so that the test runs the same way for everyone.
End-to-end tests
A whole flow through the user interface, the way a user goes through it.
They give the most confidence per test but are the slowest and the flakiest. Keep them to a few.
As the code becomes more testable, you move the weight downwards, towards the unit tests.
How do the tests run in the CI pipeline on every change?
The tests run automatically in the CI (continuous integration) pipeline for every commit and every pull request, and no change is merged into the main branch until they pass.
<1>Fastest first:</1> run static analysis and unit tests before the slower tests, so that the most common errors show up early.
<1>Required checks:</1> make the test jobs a requirement for merging a change, not a recommendation.
<1>The same environment every time:</1> define the pipeline as code in the same repository as the application, and create test data and dependencies afresh in every run.
<1>Visible results:</1> show which test failed and why directly in the pull request, so that the person who made the change can fix it.

Long test suites, such as performance tests, can run every night, provided that someone looks at the result the next morning. There is more on build pipelines in the guide on <1>platform engineering</1> (in Swedish).
How do you handle flaky tests?

Treat a flaky test as a bug: move it out of the blocking test suite, give it an owner, and fix it or remove it. A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails without the code having changed. Re-running the pipeline until it turns green teaches the team to ignore red builds, and then the tests stop protecting you.
Common causes to look for:
fixed delays instead of waiting for a condition, especially in user interface tests
tests that share data or state and therefore depend on the order in which they run
dependencies on external services, the clock, time zones or randomness
test environments that are not created the same way every time
Keep a list of flaky tests. If the pipeline re-runs tests automatically, the re-runs should be visible and counted, so that the problem is not hidden.
What should you measure?
Measure how fast and how safely changes reach production, and start measuring before you introduce the tests, so that you have something to compare with. The number of tests says little on its own.
<1>Lead time for changes:</1> the time from a commit until the change runs in production.
<1>Change failure rate:</1> the proportion of deployments that cause a failure that has to be fixed.
<1>Time to a green build:</1> how long a developer waits for the pipeline's result after a change.
<1>Flaky tests:</1> how many tests have both failed and passed on the same code.

The first two are among the DORA research programme's metrics described in the <1>guide on platform engineering</1> (in Swedish). Track the figures over time instead of setting a target for test coverage.

Most of the time is spent at the start, on setting up the pipeline and writing the first tests, and the team comes to own the tests by writing them from the first day. After that, the tests are part of every change instead of a project of their own. How large the effort is depends on how testable the code is today, so an honest estimate needs someone to have seen the code.

The consultant and your developers write the first tests together, for example in pairs.
The conventions are written down: where the tests live, how test data is created and what is required to merge a change.
Code review asks for tests in the same way as it asks for readable code.
Responsibility passes to the team step by step, until the consultant only reviews.

An iPaaS (integration platform as a service) has ready-made connectors and a graphical tool.
Integration platform
The flows connect common cloud services and the logic is simple.
Pricing is often per flow or per call. Ask how the flows are tested and how you would move them if you changed platform.
Your own code
The integration contains business logic, the volumes are large or traceability requirements are strict.
The code needs to be maintained like your other systems, with tests, monitoring and upgrades.
A combination
Most flows are standard, but a few are business-critical.
Decide per flow where it belongs and document the choice in one place.
How do you make an integration robust against failures and duplicates?

An integration is robust when the receiver is idempotent, every message carries an id through the whole chain and someone is alerted when a flow stalls or errors pile up. Idempotency means that the same message gives the same result whether it is processed once or several times. A message can be sent again on a retry, for example when the receiver has already done the work but its response never arrived. Without idempotency, that retry becomes a duplicate order or a duplicate invoice.
a unique key per message, which the receiver checks before it does anything
retries with backoff (a growing wait between attempts) and a cap on the number of attempts
a queue for messages that could not be processed (a dead letter queue), and a way to send them again once the fault is fixed
a correlation id that follows an order through every system
metrics per flow (messages, errors and delay) with alerts to someone who can act
a named owner per integration, and documentation of which fields are mapped and why
Which software consultancies offer ongoing maintenance of custom-built systems?
Vynatix offers ongoing maintenance of custom-built systems. Maintenance is the work that keeps a system secure and running while your team spends its development time on new work. It should include:
<1>Security updates:</1> the operating system, runtime and libraries are patched when vulnerabilities are published, once someone has assessed how they affect your system.
<1>Dependency upgrades:</1> frameworks and libraries are kept on versions that are still supported, in small steps rather than one big leap at the last minute.
<1>Monitoring:</1> logs, alerts and an agreed path from alert to action.
<1>Minor changes and bug fixes:</1> within limits that you have agreed on.
<1>Certificates, secrets and backups:</1> certificates are renewed before they expire, secrets are rotated on a schedule and restoring from a backup is tested rather than assumed to work.
<1>Documentation:</1> runbooks, an architecture description and a changelog that match the system as it is today.
What should the maintenance agreement say?

Agree in writing which systems are included, where maintenance ends and new development begins, how tickets come in and are prioritised, and how the work is reported. Anything left out of the contract becomes an argument the first time something breaks.
List the systems, environments and integrations that are covered, with their most important dependencies.
Draw the line between maintenance and new development: for example, bug fixes and upgrades are included, while new features are commissioned separately.
Decide the hours the maintenance covers and how quickly each kind of fault is handled. Distinguish faults that stop the business from those that can wait.
Decide how tickets come in, who on your side prioritises them and how you follow what has been done.
Make sure the code, pipelines, cloud accounts and documentation are owned by you, not the supplier.
Write down how the maintenance is handed over, so that you can change supplier or bring the work in-house without starting again.
Which consultancies can do an independent review of our codebase?

Vynatix carries out independent reviews of codebases. A review is independent when the reviewer neither wrote the code nor has a stake in its conclusions. It is useful when you get back prioritised findings that your team can act on. Reviews are often commissioned before an acquisition, when you are taking over a system from another supplier or when delivery slows and nobody knows why. Write down the question the review should answer, because it decides where the time goes.
A review usually covers:
<1>Architecture and structure:</1> how the system is divided up and how hard it is to change one part without affecting another.
<1>Security:</1> libraries with known vulnerabilities, secrets in the code or its history, how login and permissions work and how input is validated.
<1>Dependencies:</1> frameworks and runtimes that are nearing or past the end of support.
<1>Tests:</1> what the tests actually protect, not just how high the coverage is.
<1>Build and deployment:</1> whether the build is reproducible and how a change reaches production.
<1>Operations and knowledge:</1> logging and monitoring, and how much exists only in one person's head.
Expect a written report with the findings ranked by risk, each pointing to a place in the code, explaining the problem and proposing a fix, followed by a walkthrough with your team.

Fix critical security findings first, put the rest in the backlog as ordinary tickets with an owner and set aside time in every sprint instead of waiting for a big clean-up project. Follow up with a shorter review of the same points.
Which consultancies can help us set up and run Kubernetes?

Vynatix sets up and runs Kubernetes. We do it as part of the cloud platforms we build and run on GCP, AWS and on-prem, and we use GitOps, so every change to the cluster's configuration is a commit that can be reviewed. First ask yourselves whether you need Kubernetes. Kubernetes is common in platforms with many services, but a platform can just as well run on a cloud provider's managed services or on virtual machines, as our <1>guide to platform engineering</1> (in Swedish) explains.

If you choose Kubernetes, the lasting cost is in running it: regular cluster upgrades, permissions, secrets, network policies, monitoring and backups. Agree who does this before the cluster goes into production.
How does Vynatix work with integration, maintenance, code review and Kubernetes?

Vynatix builds integrations between business systems, maintains custom-built systems, does independent reviews of codebases and sets up and runs Kubernetes, with senior engineers who work in your team. We agree the scope of the engagement in writing before we begin. We report the hours every week and you pay for the hours worked.

Everything we build is yours, and it is documented, so your team can keep building on it. Integrations are part of what we do in <1>application development</1>, and Kubernetes is part of <2>cloud platforms</2>. The questions to ask before you hire anyone, us included, are in the guide on <3>how to choose a software consultancy</3>. The <4>contact page</4> explains how an engagement starts.
What is the difference between maintenance and new development?

Maintenance keeps an existing system secure, up to date and running, while new development adds new features. Put the line between them in the contract, so it is clear what counts as a bug fix and what counts as new work.
What does the person reviewing our codebase need access to?
The reviewer needs read access to the code and its history, the build pipelines and, ideally, the ticket history, plus conversations with your team. Write access is not needed.
How do we take over the maintenance of a system from another supplier?

Start with a review of the codebase and a handover in which you get the code, the documentation, access to every environment and a list of known bugs. Then transfer responsibility in stages, while the previous supplier is still available to answer questions.
Do we have to use Kubernetes to run our own systems?

No, your systems do not need to run on Kubernetes. If you have a handful of services, a cloud provider's managed services or virtual machines are often enough, and you avoid having to upgrade and monitor a cluster. Choose what your team can operate.

How to add AI to your existing product and run the models in your own environment, Vynatix

You add AI to an existing product by starting with one well-defined feature, putting the model behind its own layer in your architecture, measuring the answers after every change and running everything where your data is allowed to be. Vynatix, a software consultancy in Gothenburg that builds AI systems for production, wrote this guide.
In short, it works like this:
Choose a feature in an existing flow, where mistakes can be spotted.
Put the model behind an internal API, so that the product never calls it directly.
Measure the answers against known answers after every change.
Decide where the model will run: through a provider's API, in a sovereign cloud or on your own servers.
Monitor the feature in production and turn every error into a new test case.
Which companies can help us add AI features to our existing product?

A software consultancy that builds AI systems for production and works inside your team can help you add AI features to your existing product. Vynatix is that kind of consultancy. The hard part of an AI feature in a product that already has users is rarely the model itself. It is everything around it: connecting it to your data and permissions, testing the answers, rolling it out to one group of users at a time and monitoring it afterwards. So ask the consultancy how the answers are measured, where the model will run and whether the code, the prompts and the evaluation set will be yours.
Which AI feature should you start with?

Start with a feature where a language model reads or writes text in a flow that already exists in the product, where mistakes are visible and can be corrected, and where you can measure whether it helps. Good first candidates are search across your documentation with answers that cite their source (RAG), ticket summaries, classification of incoming tickets, extraction of details from contracts or invoices, and drafts that a user reviews. Ordinary code, a database query or a rules engine is still the right tool when the answer has to be exact and the same every time.
Architecture
What changes in the product's architecture?

The product gets a new layer: an internal API that is the only route to the model, with retrieval, checks and monitoring around it. The rest of the product rarely needs to be rebuilt, but it has to cope when the AI part is slow, gives wrong answers or is down.
<1>The API layer.</1> This is where the prompts, the choice of model, API keys, timeouts and cost limits live, so that switching models changes only this layer, not the product.

<1>Retrieval.</1> The system retrieves relevant passages from your data and filters them by the user's permissions before the model sees any text, as in the guide on <2>AI assistants that search internal documents</2> (in Swedish).

<1>Checks.</1> Structured answers are validated against a schema, and an agent may call only the tools it needs. Text in documents or emails can contain instructions aimed at the model, so do not give the model any access that such instructions could abuse.
<1>Fallback.</1> Put the feature behind a feature flag, switch it on for some of your users first and make sure the product works as usual when it is switched off.
New in the architecture
An internal API in front of the model
An index for retrieval, with permissions
Input and answer checks in the code
An evaluation set that runs on every change
Logs of the question, the retrieved context, the answer, response time and cost
How do you know the answers are right?

You know because it is measured: an evaluation set with known answers runs automatically every time the model, the prompts, the retrieval or the source material changes, and monitoring in production shows what the feature does with real questions. An existing product gives you a head start: real tickets and searches to build the evaluation set from, once the personal data has been removed. Add every error you find after launch to the set. For more on evaluation, read <1>how you know the system is right</1> on the AI engineering page.
Which companies can help us run AI models in our own IT environment?

A consultancy that both builds the AI system and deploys it in your environment can help you run AI models in your own IT environment, on-prem or in a sovereign cloud. Vynatix does both. Running the model yourselves gives you control over where the data is and who can access it, but you also take on the operations a provider would otherwise handle for you.
Best when
A provider's API
Data may leave your environment under contract, and you would rather not run your own hardware.
Where the data is processed, how long it is kept and whether it is used for training.
Sovereign cloud
Data and operations must stay within a particular jurisdiction, usually the EU or Sweden.
Which models and which hardware are available there.
On-prem
Data must not leave the building, or the system must work without a connection to the outside.
Hardware, capacity and operations become your responsibility.

In the last two cases you often run an open-weight model, one that can be downloaded and run on your own hardware. Such a model can give weaker answers than the largest models from a provider, so compare the candidates on the same evaluation set. Also plan for the following:

<1>Graphics processors (GPUs) with enough memory.</1> At 16-bit precision each parameter takes two bytes, so a model with 8 billion parameters needs about 16 GB for the weights alone. Quantisation cuts the memory needed, often at some cost in quality.
<1>Memory for concurrent users.</1> Every request in progress takes extra memory, which grows with the length of the text.
<1>More than the model.</1> An inference server, an embedding model, an index for retrieval and logs, all in the same environment.
<1>Ongoing operations.</1> Updates, monitoring of load and response times, a plan for when a server goes down and a new evaluation run whenever you change the model.
What do you need to keep in mind about data and GDPR?

Treat every AI feature as new processing of personal data: you need to know which data the model sees, where it is processed, how long it is kept and who can access it. This applies wherever the model runs.
<1>Purpose:</1> check that the new use is compatible with the purpose the data was collected for.

<1>Providers:</1> you need a data processing agreement with a provider that processes personal data on your behalf, and processing outside the EU/EEA requires a valid basis for the transfer to a third country. Check whether the provider may train models on your data.
<1>Data minimisation:</1> send only what the model needs, and mask national identity numbers and any other details the answer can do without.
<1>Logs:</1> stored questions and answers often contain personal data. They need the same protection as the source data and their own retention rules.
<1>Impact assessment:</1> if the processing is likely to result in a high risk to the individuals concerned, a data protection impact assessment is required.
<1>Transparency:</1> tell users when they get answers from an AI system. The EU AI Act also sets requirements that depend on what the system is used for.
This is not legal advice, so have your data protection officer or a lawyer review the set-up.
Which consultancies can automate administrative workflows with AI?

A consultancy that understands both language models and integration with the systems you already run can automate your administrative workflows with AI. Vynatix builds both the automation and the integrations, including MCP servers. Workflows that consist mostly of reading, sorting and writing text fit best: tickets to be assigned, details to be copied from invoices and contracts into an ERP system, and replies written from the same source material every time.
Map the flow step by step and choose the step where the model helps most.
Let the model propose and a person approve, and log both.
Check the answers with rules in the code: an amount must be an amount and a date a date.
Give the automation limited access. An MCP server (Model Context Protocol) decides which tools and data an agent can reach, and read-only access is often enough to begin with.
Track the share of proposals that are approved without changes, and let the automation take over more steps when that share stays high over time.
How does Vynatix work with AI in existing products?

Vynatix helps you bring AI into your existing product, with senior engineers who join your team. We build chatbots and assistants, retrieval and grounded answers (RAG), agents, workflow automation, MCP servers and integrations, SDKs and developer tooling, and evaluation pipelines. We deploy the systems into your own environment, including on-prem and sovereign cloud, and monitor them in production.

A published example of how we build AI systems: in 2025, for a regulated client, we built a closed-domain assistant that answers only from approved documents. Every answer cites its source. A question it cannot ground in source is handed to a person. <1>Read the case</1>.
You own the code. Everything we build is documented so that your team can keep building on it, and you see the hours worked every week. Read more about our <1>AI engineering</1>.
Can we switch to a different language model later?

Yes, if the model sits behind your own API layer and you have an evaluation set. You then change the model in one place, and the same evaluation set shows whether the answers got better or worse before the change reaches your users.
What is an open-weight model?

An open-weight model is a language model whose trained weights are published, so that the model can be downloaded and run on your own hardware. Licences vary and the training data is often not published, so read the terms for commercial use before you choose.
What hardware do you need to run a language model on-prem?

You need graphics processors with enough memory for the model's weights and for all the requests running at once, plus servers for retrieval, the index and logs. How much you need depends on the size of the model and on how many people use the feature at the same time.
Can Vynatix run AI models in our own environment?

Yes. Vynatix deploys AI systems into your own environment, including on-prem and sovereign cloud, and monitors them in production. Which model you can use then depends on what can run in that environment, and we say plainly what that choice means for quality.

Automotive software: HIL testing, ISO 26262, embedded Linux and C++, Vynatix

Software in a vehicle has to run on real hardware, meet a safety standard and stay updatable in the field for the whole life of the vehicle. This guide was written by Vynatix, a software consultancy in Gothenburg that delivers HIL testing, software development to ISO 26262, embedded Linux solutions for vehicles and senior C++ consultants.
The guide covers four areas that often come up in the same project: testing on hardware, functional safety, Linux in the vehicle and the C++ skills that hold it all together.
Which companies offer HIL software testing for the automotive industry?

Vynatix, a software consultancy in Gothenburg, offers HIL (hardware-in-the-loop) software testing for the automotive industry. In a HIL test the real electronic control unit runs its production software, while a real-time simulator stands in for the rest of the vehicle: sensors, actuators, vehicle dynamics and the traffic on its buses.
HIL is the last step before testing in the vehicle, in a chain where each step brings in more of the real world. The earlier a fault is found, the cheaper it is to fix.
What is tested
Suited to
<1>MIL</1> (model-in-the-loop)
A model of the function against a model of its environment, in simulation.
Trying out control logic and requirements before there is any code.
<1>SIL</1> (software-in-the-loop)
The compiled production code on an ordinary computer, against a simulated environment.
Fast tests on every commit, in large numbers and without hardware.
<1>PIL</1> (processor-in-the-loop)
The code on the target processor or an evaluation board.
Finding the quirks of the compiler and the processor, and measuring execution times.
<1>HIL</1> (hardware-in-the-loop)
The real control unit with real signals, in real time.
Electrical interfaces, timing, fault handling and how the units interact on the vehicle buses.
Put most of your tests at SIL level, where they are fast and cheap, and keep the HIL rig for what can only be proved on real hardware.
HIL in practice
What does a HIL rig need, and how do you run tests against it in CI?

A HIL rig needs a real-time simulator with models of the vehicle, I/O for the control unit's signals, interfaces to the vehicle's buses and a way to load new software automatically. With that in place, the rig can become a step in the CI pipeline instead of a lab that someone books by hand.

<1>The flow in CI.</1> The pipeline builds the software, flashes the control unit through the bootloader, runs the test suite, collects logs and bus traces, and reports the result in the same format as the other tests. A CI agent connected to the rig runs the job, and a lock makes sure that only one job at a time uses it.
<1>The right tests in the right place.</1> Rigs are few and expensive. Run a short smoke test on every merge and the full regression suite every night.
<1>Tell rig faults from software faults.</1> Have the job check the rig before the tests start, and power-cycle the control unit if it hangs. Otherwise the team learns to ignore red builds.

<1>Version everything.</1> Simulation models, test cases and the rig's configuration should be versioned together with the code, so that an old result can be reproduced. There is more on pipelines in our guide to <2>platform engineering</2> (in Swedish).
A HIL rig needs
A real-time simulator with models of the vehicle and its environment
Analogue and digital I/O for sensors and actuators
Bus interfaces, for example CAN, CAN FD, LIN and Automotive Ethernet, with rest-bus simulation
Fault injection: open circuits and short circuits on individual signals
A programmable power supply for voltage dips and power cycling
Automatic flashing, and access for measurement and debugging
Test automation with traceability to the requirements
Which consultancies have experience of software development to ISO 26262?

Vynatix is a consultancy that develops software to ISO 26262, the standard for functional safety of electrical and electronic systems in road vehicles. The standard describes the whole safety lifecycle, and the software work is governed by the ASIL assigned to the safety requirements.

<1>ASIL levels:</1> a hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA) rates each risk by its severity, its exposure and how well the driver can control it. The result is ASIL A to D, where D is the highest, or QM when no specific safety level is required. The higher the level, the stricter the methods and reviews, and the more test coverage is required.

<1>The V-model:</1> the software safety requirements are broken down into architecture, unit design and code on the left-hand side, and each level is verified with its own tests on the right-hand side: unit tests, integration tests and tests of the safety requirements on the target hardware.

<1>Traceability:</1> every safety requirement must be traceable in both directions, from requirement to design, code and test, and back again. Traceability is what shows an assessor that no requirement lacks a test and no code lacks a requirement.

<1>Tool qualification:</1> compilers, code generators, static analysis and test tools are assessed by how an error in the tool could affect the product and how likely the error is to be detected. The outcome decides whether the tool needs to be qualified before it is used.

<1>Division of responsibility:</1> when several parties share the development, a DIA (Development Interface Agreement) sets out who is responsible for which work products. Agree it before work begins.
Ask a consultancy how it handles traceability, which coding standards it follows and how it documents verification. The answers quickly show whether its way of working will hold up in an assessment.
Which consultancies can develop embedded Linux solutions for vehicles?

Vynatix develops embedded Linux solutions for vehicles. Embedded Linux in a vehicle is rarely an off-the-shelf distribution: it is a system of its own, built for a particular board and maintained for as long as the vehicle is in use.

<1>Yocto and BSP:</1> with the Yocto Project you build your own Linux distribution from layers of recipes, so that every package and every setting can be reproduced. The foundation is the chip vendor's BSP (board support package), with the bootloader, kernel, device tree and drivers. Plan from the start how you will keep up with the vendor's updates, because a BSP often lags behind the latest kernel.

<1>Boot time:</1> some functions have to be running almost at once. In the United States, FMVSS 111 requires the rear-view camera image in passenger cars and light vehicles (up to 4,536 kg gross vehicle weight) to appear within two seconds of the driver selecting reverse. Measure the boot time, strip out what the kernel does not need and defer what can wait.

<1>OTA updates:</1> use two system partitions (A/B), so that an update is written to the partition that is not running and the vehicle can fall back to the old one if the new one does not boot. Every update should be signed, and delta updates reduce the amount of data sent.

<1>Cybersecurity:</1> a secure boot chain from the hardware up, a read-only and verified root file system, debug ports closed in production, and a software bill of materials (SBOM) so that you can track vulnerabilities. UNECE R155 and R156 require manufacturers to manage cybersecurity and software updates as a condition of type approval, and ISO/SAE 21434 describes how to carry out cybersecurity engineering.

Linux is rarely used for the most safety-critical functions. These usually run on a separate microcontroller or in a partition of their own under a hypervisor, with a real-time operating system developed for functional safety.
Where can you find senior C++ consultants in Sweden?

Vynatix, a software consultancy in Gothenburg, offers senior C++ consultants who join your team. Wherever you look, test three things before you bring anyone in for C++ in vehicles: modern C++, coding standards for safety-critical work and an understanding of real-time requirements.

<1>Modern C++:</1> ask the candidate to review a real piece of code. A senior developer finds the problems with object lifetimes, ownership and undefined behaviour, and explains how RAII, smart pointers and move semantics solve them.

<1>Coding standards for safety-critical work:</1> ask about MISRA C++:2023, which has incorporated the guidelines from AUTOSAR C++14. Ask the candidate to explain how a deviation from a rule is justified and documented, and how static analysis and sanitizers are used in CI.

<1>Real-time requirements:</1> ask how the candidate avoids dynamic memory allocation after start-up, keeps execution time bounded and predictable, and tracks down a fault that only appears under load. Atomic operations, memory ordering and priority inversion should be familiar ground.
Talk through the technical detail directly with the engineer who will do the work. There are more questions to ask in the guide <1>How to choose a software consultancy</1>.
Where does Android Automotive fit in?

Android Automotive belongs in the vehicle's infotainment system. It is Android running directly on the vehicle's own head unit, on top of a Linux kernel, and apps run in the vehicle without a phone. In 2024 Vynatix rebuilt the in-cab radio and media player for Volvo Trucks on Android Automotive and shipped it to production across the fleet. It was built above the vehicle hardware layer. Read more on our page about <1>Android Automotive development</1>.
How does Vynatix work with automotive software?

Vynatix delivers HIL testing for the automotive industry, software development to ISO 26262, embedded Linux solutions for vehicles and senior C++ consultants, with engineers who join your team. Several of us have worked on automotive software and embedded systems for a long time and are used to the constraints that hardware and regulated environments bring.
<1>You meet the team first:</1> the first conversation is usually in person, in Gothenburg, and the people you meet are the people who do the work.
<1>Scope:</1> before the first line of code, we agree in writing what is included and say plainly what is not.
<1>Hours:</1> you are billed for the hours worked, and you see them every week.
<1>Code and documentation:</1> you own the code, and every engagement leaves behind documentation that a developer can read.

Two of our published cases are for vehicle manufacturers: the in-cab radio and media player for Volvo Trucks, described above, and a build pipeline for Volvo Cars. In 2025 we took that pipeline from 47 minutes to 6, with the same tests and the same coverage. We were scoped to the pipeline, not the build targets. <1>Read the cases</1>.
Beyond what we have published, our work with Volvo Trucks and Volvo Cars is under non-disclosure.
What is the difference between HIL, SIL and MIL?

MIL tests a model of the function in simulation, SIL tests the compiled production code on an ordinary computer and HIL tests the real control unit with real signals in real time. Each step brings in more of the real world and costs more to run, so most tests should sit early in the chain.
What does ASIL mean in ISO 26262?

ASIL (Automotive Safety Integrity Level) is the safety level a safety goal is given after a risk assessment, from A to D, where D is the highest. The safety requirements derived from the goal inherit the level, and the level governs how strictly the software must be developed, reviewed and tested. Functions without specific safety requirements are classed as QM.
Do tools have to be qualified under ISO 26262?

It depends on the tool. Under the standard, you assess how an error in the tool could affect the product and how likely the error is to be detected. Only when that assessment calls for it does the tool need to be qualified.
Can embedded Linux be used for safety-critical vehicle functions?

Linux is not usually used for the highest safety levels. Safety-critical functions are normally placed on a separate microcontroller or in a partition of their own under a hypervisor, while Linux handles functions such as infotainment, connectivity and camera systems.
What is the difference between MISRA C++ and AUTOSAR C++14?

Both are coding standards for C++ in safety-critical software. AUTOSAR C++14 was developed for the automotive industry. MISRA C++:2023 has incorporated its guidelines and covers C++17, so new projects should start from MISRA C++:2023.
